items.title: Mercedes set pace in eventful Qatar second practice
items.content: <article>World champion Kimi Antonelli sets the pace ahead of Mercedes team-mate George Russell in a disrupted second practice at the Qatar Grand Prix. </article>
items.lbText:
World champion Kimi Antonelli set the pace ahead of Mercedes team-mate George Russell in a disrupted second practice at the Qatar Grand Prix.

Italian Antonelli was 0.127 seconds quicker than Russell on the medium tyre, as neither driver set a time on the soft compound because of two red flags that punctuated the session.

Lewis Hamilton also came to halt after his Ferrari lost power, with a virtual safety car deployed so the marshals could come to the seven-time world champion's aid.

The McLarens of Lando Norris and Oscar Piastri plus Red Bull's Max Verstappen completed the top five at the Lusail International Circuit, with the trio setting soft-tyre times that were more than four tenths adrift of the two Mercedes.

The first red flag was to clear gravel off the track after an incident for Ferrari's Charles Leclerc early on, while the other was to recover the Alpine of Pierre Gasly following a high-speed spin.

Frenchman Gasly hit a marker board before beaching himself after taking too much kerb at Turn 14 in the middle of the qualifying simulation runs.

The interruptions led to the second hour being extended by 13 minutes to allow drivers more time on track in the representative conditions.

"It was a productive day," said Antonelli. "We tried a lot of things on the car between FP1 and FP2, but in FP2, it seemed like we did a step back with the car.

"But it was very interesting to see how the car behaved after those changes. It's not easy."

Antonelli, who secured his maiden title in Mexico City earlier this month, was also fastest in the opening session on the mediums. Mercedes did fit the 20-year-old with the soft tyre in the first hour, but he failed to set a lap time on them.

He said he feels it will be close between himself and Russell for the race victory, but added: "You can never write off Max [Verstappen] and the others."

Norris, meanwhile, said Mercedes "were in a different category" to McLaren, highlighting the Silver Arrows "were quicker in every single corner by miles".

The 2025 world champion added: "We seem in a relatively decent position, similar on pace with Red Bull, and similar-ish to Ferrari. So I'd say it's OK."

Four-time title winner Verstappen said it had been a "difficult day" following his issues with heavy steering towards the end of the session.

"The balance of the car is probably too disconnected at the moment to go fast," he added. "It's costing us quite a bit of lap time."

Hamilton also had a moment with Verstappen that was noted by the race control. The Briton was on a flying lap when he got too close to the Dutchman, who was on a long run.

Verstappen said Hamilton had moved under braking, but the stewards decided no further investigation was needed.

The second Red Bull of Isack Hadjar was sixth on the timesheets, with Leclerc leading Hamilton in seventh and eighth, 1.3 seconds away from Antonelli's time.

The two Racing Bulls of British rookie Arvid Lindblad and Liam Lawson were ninth and 10th.

Leclerc had to head back into the garage after spinning and going through the gravel when Lawson was just ahead of him at Turn Nine.

The Monegasque driver said the car did not feel right, and the Italian team spent a chunk of time repairing the damage to the floor. After the session he said he lost control after going a little bit early on the throttle.

Ferrari arrived in Qatar after another on-track incident between Leclerc and Hamilton, this time in Las Vegas. The pair made contact and Leclerc was given a 10-second penalty for the incident, with Hamilton saying on Thursday the team were facing "very, very challenging times".

Leclerc thinks this weekend could potentially be another struggle for the Italian team, who can secure second in the constructors' championship if they can retain at least a 44-point lead over third-placed Red Bull.

"A very, very difficult day. Not even on high fuel were we strong," said Leclerc.

"We are working hard but for some reason, Mercedes is so much faster than I think everyone expected. So the gaps are just a little bit strange."

Drivers will be limited to a maximum of 27 laps on a set of tyres at the Lusail circuit, meaning teams will have to make at least two pit stops during the 57-lap grand prix on Sunday, which starts at 16:00 GMT.

The decision is caused by concern over the integrity of the Pirelli tyres on the high-speed, 16-corner track. Laps to the grid, formation laps and any laps completed after the end of the race will not be included.

Hamilton was told by his engineer in first practice tyre degradation was "much higher than expected" after highlighting his own issues.

Qatar and next week's finale in Abu Dhabi are going ahead as planned despite the ongoing conflict between the United States/Israel and Iran.

Round 22 of the 2026 Formula 1 season heads to the Lusail International Circuit for the Qatar Grand Prix, from 27-29 November.

Red Bull's Max Verstappen finished on the top step of the podium in a chaotic Las Vegas Grand Prix which featured 352 overtakes.

The Dutchman was joined on the podium by McLaren's Lando Norris in second and Oscar Piastri in third.

Ferrari missed out on the chance to secure second in the constructors' championship after Charles Leclerc made contact with team-mate Lewis Hamilton.

items.title: Ferrari facing 'very challenging times' - Hamilton
items.content: <article>Lewis Hamilton says Ferrari are facing "very, very challenging times" as a result of the series of on-track incidents between himself and team-mate Charles Leclerc.</article>
items.lbText:
Lewis Hamilton says Ferrari are facing "very, very challenging times" as a result of the series of on-track incidents between himself and team-mate Charles Leclerc.

The two drivers had talks on Thursday after arriving at the Qatar Grand Prix to discuss the fall-out from their collision in the race in Las Vegas last weekend, which team boss Frederic Vasseur said was "completely unacceptable" .

Both said the conclusion of those discussions would "stay internal" but admitted a solution needed to be found.

Hamilton said: "I like to think that we're stronger from these difficult...

"If everything was just great all the time, I don't think you learn anything when you're winning all the time. You learn really through the hardest times.

"These are definitely very, very challenging times for Fred and Charles and I."

Is Hamilton and Leclerc's Ferrari partnership sustainable? F1 Q&A

Hamilton-Leclerc collision 'completely unacceptable'

Leclerc admitted that "at the moment it's not working" and said there was "tension around that we need to dissipate".

The incident in Las Vegas was the second in three races between Hamilton and Leclerc .

In Mexico City last month, their battle on the first lap led to them handing victory to Red Bull's Max Verstappen in a race that Ferrari should have finished one-two.

After that event. Hamilton said Ferrari "had to have some serious talks behind closed doors" and that the team had "big, big problems".

They had those talks in the next race in Brazil, brokered by Vasseur, only for there to be two flashpoints in Las Vegas.

Hamilton was first penalised 10 seconds for gaining an advantage by cutting the track while racing with McLaren's Lando Norris, in an incident to which Leclerc was also in close proximity.

And then Leclerc received a 10-second penalty for pitching Hamilton into a spin.

Leclerc said: "We have a very good relationship outside the car with Lewis.

"I wouldn't say the atmosphere was good because we are disappointed by the situation we are in.

"But we are all grown up and responsible and we have to find a solution and there is also a big willingness to find a solution."

Leclerc said the incidents kept happening because "we are two very strong drivers who want to finish one ahead of the other".

He added: "I do believe some level of tension is always there in top teams when you have two drivers.

"If you look this year there have been more than 10 times we have started side by side. We are always together. So a certain amount of tension is obviously always there, but it doesn't necessarily have to escalate and that is why we need to find a solution and fix that."

Hamilton added: "I have no doubts that next year we'll come back working hard together and in a better place. I think we'll quickly get better processes in place so that we can really get a right team."

Russell says Verstappen's criticism 'quite amusing'

items.title: Russell finds Verstappen's criticism 'quite amusing'
items.content: <article>George Russell says Max Verstappen can "say what he wants" and that he found the Red Bull driver's criticisms of him after the Las Vegas Grand Prix "quite amusing".</article>
items.lbText:
George Russell has said Max Verstappen can "say what he wants" and explained he found the Red Bull driver's criticisms of him after the Las Vegas Grand Prix "quite amusing".

Verstappen said Russell was "so far below my level" after winning the race on Saturday.

His remarks were a response to Mercedes driver Russell saying "somebody has to stand up to this guy" after an on-track confrontation in practice.

Russell said before this weekend's penultimate grand prix of the season in Qatar: "I stand by what I said after practice, but he was the one who went out and won the race and I didn't, and I'm sure he had a bit of a laugh about that and it was reasonably amusing.

"He drove an incredible race and won it and he can afford to say what he wants."

Russell v Verstappen: F1’s New Rivalry Explodes in Vegas

Is Hamilton and Leclerc's Ferrari partnership sustainable? F1 Q&A

Asked whether he wanted to pursue reconciliation with Dutchman Verstappen, Russell said: "We're all competitors out there. There's no right or wrong way about the mentality everybody has.

"We are all different in many regards and you don't need to agree with one another. I'm not looking to be best mates with anybody on the grid. I am just working and looking and fighting to win. Simple as that."

British driver Russell said he had learned lessons from the incident in Vegas, which is the latest in a series of flashpoints between himself and four-time champion Verstappen dating back several years, and he might change how open he is with the media in future.

"It's all avoidable at the end of the day," Russell said. "It's all a bit unnecessary. It's not something I am looking to continue. I am not looking to have a poor relationship with people. That's not really the kind of person I am.

"There are lessons to be taken from these situations. Maybe I am just too open and honest with the media. I need to remember I'm talking to a camera that is broadcasting to millions of people. That's the biggest takeaway.

"It is not a war of words off track. I maybe have been guilty of being too open and honest when I speak with you guys.

"I feel like I have a good relationship with the media and I sometimes forget I am not talking to one person - I am talking to millions of people on the television.

"That good relationship has probably hindered me a bit and that is life lessons. I respect Max immensely for his driving talent and what he has achieved on track."

items.title: Bearman to continue with Haas in 2027
items.content: <article>Britain's Oliver Bearman will continue to race for the Haas team in Formula 1 in 2027.</article>
items.lbText:
Britain's Oliver Bearman will continue to race for the Haas team in Formula 1 in 2027.

The US-based team announced the 21-year-old's new deal on Thursday, at the start of the Qatar Grand Prix weekend.

It marks Bearman's third full season with Haas, for whom he first raced for two one-off events in 2024 before becoming a full-time driver in 2025.

The announcement ends a protracted negotiation period in which Bearman's management were seeking reassurances about his future from Ferrari.

Bearman is a member of the Italian team's driver academy and has ambitions to race for Ferrari in the future.

It was not immediately clear what reassurances Bearman had been given about his future by Ferrari.

Is Hamilton and Leclerc's Ferrari partnership sustainable? F1 Q&A

Camara to continue with Haas for final two races

Haas team principal Ayao Komatsu said: "Continuing with Ollie into 2027 was a natural decision for us.

"We've seen his growth, his commitment, and the quality he brings to the team, both on and off the track.

"He has a tremendous work ethic and a strong desire to develop both himself and the team, and there is no better person, in my opinion, to lead this team forward."

Bearman added: "It's no secret that I'm delighted to be continuing with Haas into 2027.

"This team has played an integral role in my development, and I've felt a huge amount of belief and support from everyone here.

"We've got big ambitions to keep pushing forward, and I'm excited to lead that work, building on what we've achieved, and striving for even more together – we have unfinished business."

Bearman will be partnered at Haas next season with Brazilian Rafael Camara, who is also a member of the Ferrari driver academy.

Camara has started racing for Haas at the end of this season, following the team's sacking of Frenchman Esteban Ocon midway through the Mexico City Grand Prix weekend.

Bearman's concerns about his future had been rooted in the fact that there might not be a seat available at Ferrari for some considerable time.

Charles Leclerc is on a long-term contract there, and while Lewis Hamilton's deal is believed to end after 2027, the seven-time champion is keen to continue in F1 for a number more years.

Bearman, who said at last weekend's Las Vegas Grand Prix, that he was "quite disappointed" his new contract had not yet been sorted so late in the season, is believed to have been exploring his options.

His management is said to have been asking Ferrari for reassurances about his future, either about the possibility of racing for the main team, or if that is not an option, being allowed to pursue a career at a more competitive team than Haas.

items.title: Williams exceeded F1 cost cap by £627,000
items.content: <article>Williams "unintentially" broke Formula 1's cost cap during the 2025 season, governing body the FIA finds.</article>
items.lbText:
Williams broke Formula 1's cost cap during the 2025 season, governing body the FIA has found.

The team say they "unintentionally" exceeded the cap by £627,000. Last season, the spending limit was $135m (£106m).

Alpine were also found to have broken the rules, although theirs was a procedural breach without overspending.

Both teams have reached so-called 'accepted breach agreements' with the FIA.

Williams' involves a financial penalty, the amount of which has not been disclosed, and a 1.5% reduction in permitted aerodynamic research and development time for the next 12 months.

Alpine have also been given an undisclosed financial penalty.

Both teams must foot the costs of the investigations by the FIA into their rule-breaking.

A Williams statement said: "The breach relates to administrative costs we incurred making changes to our company structure.

"We believed these costs fell outside of the cap. Following discussions with the FIA, we have agreed to resolve the matter in line with their interpretation that the costs should have been in cap.

"The FIA has noted that Williams did not gain any sporting or financial advantage, and nor did we ever seek to. It has also noted that we acted co-operatively and in good faith throughout the review process.

"Integrity is central to what Williams stands for and we can now close this case and remain focused on our future."

The FIA said in a statement: "There is no accusation or evidence that (Williams) sought at any time to act in bad faith, dishonestly or in a fraudulent manner, nor that it wilfully concealed any information from the cost-cap administration.

"The financial regulations are complex, and the breaches arose from an interpretation adopted by (Williams) in good faith.

"Williams has accepted the FIA's interpretation and the resulting breaches."

It said Williams' breach was the equivalent of a 0.48% overspend, which "falls at the lower end of the less than 5% minor overspend range".

Williams' costs were incurred as the team tried to update their operations in order to become more competitive.

Williams had targeted the new 2026 regulations as an opportunity to make a significant step forwards in the team's attempt to return to the front of F1.

Instead, the team have taken a step backwards, and after finishing fifth in 2025, are lying ninth in the constructors' championship with two races remaining this season.

Alpine said in a statement: "The team accepts that it unknowingly committed a procedural breach, which is a result of inaccuracies in the full-year reporting documentation for costs related to exclusions and adjustments.

"The errors and inaccuracies in the reporting were specifically related to non-sporting and operational costs which the CCA recognised didn't give the team any performance advantage, such as marketing activities, non-F1 activities, HR activities, employees' bonus costs, offsetting of costs, and costs of inventories."

items.title: Is Hamilton and Leclerc's Ferrari partnership sustainable? F1 Q&A
items.content: <article>BBC F1 correspondent Andrew Benson answers your latest questions after the Las Vegas Grand Prix.</article>
items.lbText:
Max Verstappen triumphed in a thrilling Las Vegas Grand Prix ahead of the McLarens of Lando Norris and Oscar Piastri.

There were 34 lead changes across the 50 laps of racing as Dutchman Verstappen held off attacks from Mercedes' Kimi Antonelli and George Russell, plus his Red Bull team-mate Isack Hadjar.

Ferrari had to deal with another intra-team battle on track as Charles Leclerc received a 10-second time penalty after colliding with Lewis Hamilton.

Here, BBC F1 correspondent Andrew Benson answers your latest questions.

Verstappen a constant amid chaos as he says Russell is 'so far below my level'

After Las Vegas, have Ferrari now reached a crossroads? With Lewis Hamilton and Charles Leclerc's on-track antics, is their partnership sustainable? Should Ferrari consider a change of direction, potentially bringing Oliver Bearman into the equation? - Michael

The battle between Lewis Hamilton and Charles Leclerc at Ferrari is one that keeps on giving - but not in a way Ferrari would want.

The collision in Las Vegas for which Leclerc was penalised was just the latest flashpoint for the team in a season that has been full of them.

The drivers argued over race strategy in relation to each other in Zandvoort and Singapore.

Hamilton made an aggressive dive down the inside at the first chicane on the first lap at Monza, only for Leclerc to shove him on to the gravel.

Hamilton ignored calls to pit in both Singapore (because he didn't want to just circulate behind Leclerc) and Brazil (because, he said, he had not been given enough information about the weather).

There was the first-lap incident at Turn Four in Mexico in which their fighting led to both going off track and letting in Max Verstappen to win a race Ferrari should have finished one-two.

And now Las Vegas, where first Hamilton earned a 10-second penalty for gaining a position on Lando Norris on track in an incident that also involved Leclerc, then Leclerc was given a 10-second penalty for tipping Hamilton into a spin later in the race.

Leclerc was on the receiving end of team principal Frederic Vasseur's ire in Las Vegas - the Frenchman calling the situation "unacceptable". But inside Ferrari they felt both drivers had a degree of culpability for the Mexico situation.

Somehow Vasseur needs to get a handle on this.

Ferrari want to allow them to race. And it's hard to imagine two drivers of such standing would accept anything else.

The problem is that doing so, amid their battle for supremacy within the team, is harming the team's results.

The concern for Ferrari is this is happening when there is relatively little at stake. It's easy to imagine how combustible it could become if Ferrari have a car capable of challenging for the title next year.

Both want to be the driver to deliver that next championship, for very different reasons.

Hamilton would get his eighth, which he feels he was unfairly denied in Abu Dhabi in 2021. And Leclerc would win his first, and complete the journey of being the first Ferrari academy driver to win the world championship for the team.

At the moment, this is not an existential question, but it's easy to see how it could become one, and Ferrari left with a decision of it being one or the other if they can't find a way to race without compromising the team.

Both drivers have buy into that and, as Lando Norris and Oscar Piastri have largely done at McLaren, accept there will be days when they have to sacrifice themselves for the greater good of Ferrari while ensuring they are ahead of the other more often than not on speed and fair racing.

It's then up to the team to decide when there comes a point to impose team orders if either or both are in a title fight with another driver.

It remains to be seen whether either of them can fully buy into that in circumstances when they individually end up losing out.

Why does George Russell often feel the need to try mind games and make comments, such as those about Max Verstappen? It often backfires on him and are usually made when he's got nothing to race for. Shouldn't he focus on himself? - Nick

This, as Mercedes team principal Toto Wolff pointed out after the race in Las Vegas, is a rivalry that goes back years.

"They've known each other so long," was Wolff's verdict. "Since karting. I think it's probably been a bit of cat and mouse. Provocations on either side. Another good factor of entertainment."

Verstappen also had a bit of a set-to with Racing Bulls' Liam Lawson in Mexico practice, which was not dissimilar in some ways.

There, stewards ruled that both had driven in an "unacceptable manner" and both drivers admitted their moves had been unnecessary and clumsy.

There's no question Russell believed what he was saying about Verstappen's driving in final practice at Las Vegas. According to the stewards, he was in the right, as Verstappen was given a warning for his changing direction in the braking zone.

Are these mind games? Or just Russell saying what he thinks? He feels he has a valid point to make.

Making it in public does not seem to affect Verstappen in any way. Does it change anything? Verstappen is a remorseless, ruthless competitor on track whether he is provoked or not.

Yes, he admitted satisfaction when he saw Russell make his late-race error in Las Vegas. But did he race any differently because of the Briton's comments? That's unlikely. Verstappen was just doing what he felt was right to win the race.

Ultimately, it's Russell's career, and it's up to him how he conducts himself, what he chooses to say in public and what he does not.

Track design, cold temperatures, energy deployment strategies or just the unwillingness of one team-mate to hold station behind another. What was the dominant factor in Las Vegas that led to such a hectic race? - Tim…

items.title: Camara to continue with Haas for final two races
items.content: <article>Brazilian Rafael Camara will continue to race for the Haas team for the final two grands prix of the Formula 1 season.</article>
items.lbText:
Brazilian Rafael Camara will continue to race for the Haas team for the final two grands prix of the Formula 1 season.

The 21-year-old, who was already signed to drive for the US-based team in 2027 , was drafted in for this month's Sao Paulo Grand Prix after Frenchman Esteban Ocon was dropped following a bust-up with team boss Ayao Komatsu.

The decision to keep Camara in the Haas seat in preparation for next season means he will likely lose the Formula 2 title.

He is leading the F2 championship by seven points from Bulgarian Nikola Tsolov heading into the final two events in Qatar and Abu Dhabi.

Komatsu said: "We're excited to be able to finish the season with Rafa driving and build on his first two race starts with the team in Brazil and America.

"I'm delighted that Rafa's embraced every track session as a learning opportunity and embedded himself further within the team.

"We now get to finish the season together which is advantageous to us all ahead of a relatively short off-season and as our 2027 preparations get under way."

A statement from Haas announcing the move did not include a quote from Camara.

items.title: Verstappen a constant amid chaos as he says Russell is 'so far below my level'
items.content: <article>Max Verstappen was the star figure in a Las Vegas Grand Prix that was unlike any F1 race anyone younger than about 70 had ever seen.</article>
items.lbText:
Warning: This article contains offensive language

Max Verstappen was a constant amid the chaos at a remarkable Las Vegas Grand Prix.

He was the star figure in a race that had 34 overtaking moves for the lead in 50 laps and 352 overall, in which the biggest advantage the leader ever had was 1.5 seconds, and in which there were five cars fighting nose to tail for the lead to the final lap, and for much of the race many more than that.

Even better for Verstappen, George Russell made a critical mistake 24 hours after he had revived his long-standing, on-off spat with the Dutchman.

Russell, who had been Verstappen's main threat from the start of the race, locked up his brakes and speared into the barrier trying to pass Mercedes team-mate Kimi Antonelli for second place behind Verstappen with two laps to go.

Verstappen said: "He speaks a lot next to the track, and it doesn't really bother me because he's so far below my level that it doesn't really make any sense for me anyway to try and challenge that, you know?

"And today, karma is a bitch. It was honestly fantastic when I looked in my mirror and I saw what was happening. I was, like, "Fantastic, my day is only getting better."

"And of course, when I then crossed the line in first, my day was complete."

Verstappen wins extraordinary race as Ferraris collide

Hamilton-Leclerc collision 'completely unacceptable'

Verstappen felt motivated to make these remarks because of what Russell had said the day before.

After an on-track altercation in practice, the pair had had an exchange of views in the stewards' room. Then, after Verstappen took pole from Russell - after fastest man Antonelli's five-place penalty was taken into account - the Briton took a pop at the Dutchman.

"I am not just going to accept somebody to screw me over like this and walk around like they are bigger and better than everyone else," Russell said. "Somebody has got to stand up to that guy."

In the paddock, a number of people felt that Verstappen was probably not the right "guy" to pick a fight with.

Even though Russell was battling with Verstappen throughout the race, the nature of their drives was different.

Russell would pass the Red Bull on the straight. Then Verstappen would reclaim the lead in more extreme fashion, on the outside of the fast kink leading on to the pit straight, or on the outside again at the long Turn Three.

Hardly anyone else even tried these moves, let alone pulled them off. Verstappen made them look routine.

After his error, Russell managed to extricate himself from the crash barrier, but he had turned a certain podium finish into a ninth place.

It was the perfect encapsulation of a season in which almost nothing has gone right.

For Verstappen, it was almost too good to be true.

The race was unlike any grand prix anyone younger than about 70 had ever seen.

The fabled slipstreaming battles of a pre-chicane Monza in the 1960s and early 1970s - that led to the closest ever finish in F1 history at the 1971 Italian Grand Prix, , external when the first five cars crossed the line 0.6secs apart - were the closest comparison at the highest echelon of the sport.

In modern terms, it was more reminiscent of American oval racing, where the high-speed nature of the race tracks leads to long chains of cars slipstreaming and lots of overtaking, little of it meaningful until the final stages.

Mercedes F1 team boss Toto Wolff pretty much hit the nail on the head when he said: "It was Indy 500 and Nascar and Formula 1 mixed - I enjoyed it."

And it encapsulated something else about F1 2026 - the internal debate that has been raging in the sport about artificiality ever since the latest engines were introduced.

The near 50-50 split between internal combustion and electrical power has created energy-starved cars where the batteries run out before the end of long straights.

On certain tracks this has led to a form of racing known as "yo-yo", where cars constantly pass and re-pass each other depending on their respective levels of battery charge.

After a chaotic few races early in the year, this has diminished as teams have better understood energy management.

But in Las Vegas the combination of long straights and slipstreaming brought it to its apotheosis. And no-one quite knew what to think about it.

Verstappen said: "Really, really surreal and something that I've never seen before in Formula 1 myself.

"It was just a crazy amount of fighting. The slipstream was so big that you - it was just impossible to drive off, and it was just crazy how many people were just following you.

"It was just very exciting, I guess, for everyone to watch. I know, of course, it's a big show around here the whole weekend, and I hope that we delivered on track."

That was a carefully judged answer for the television cameras, the sort that sounds like one thing, but if you know the person's real views, you can read between the lines to see the nuances that hint at something else.

In the news conference, Verstappen's true feelings came out. Was it a kind of racing he enjoyed?

"When I look at it from my racer heart, not," he said. "When you look at it as a show spectacle, yes.

"I enjoyed my repassing and everything, but I prefer to look at it with my racing heart. Even my heart rate, I was not nervous at all because it's just felt kind of cruising out there, just trying to press the battery whenever it was correct or defend.

"But for the show, when you look at it from the outside, probably, yes, you like it. But, yeah, I don't know.

"I probably shouldn't say it. I probably should not. I remember winning one like this when I was playing Mario Kart.

"Sometimes you drop back and you get drafts, and there's like a catch-up, you know? Always when you're dropping back, you go faster. So that's the last time that I felt something like this."

items.title: Verstappen wins extraordinary race as Ferraris collide
items.content: <article>Red Bull's Max Verstappen wins an extraordinary Las Vegas Grand Prix that featured 34 lead changes and another collision between the Ferraris.</article>
items.lbText:
Red Bull's Max Verstappen won an extraordinary Las Vegas Grand Prix that featured 34 lead changes in a non-stop battle at the front.

The leading group of 10 cars were tied together for the vast majority of the race as the lead constantly changed hands between Verstappen and the Mercedes drivers George Russell and Kimi Antonelli.

But Verstappen was the one constant, always seeming a step ahead of his rivals as he debated electrical energy deployment strategy with his team.

And in the final laps Mercedes' challenge unravelled as first Russell made a mistake and crashed trying to pass Antonelli, and the Italian lost out to the two McLarens of Lando Norris and Oscar Piastri going into the final lap.

The world champion dropped to fifth going on to the Strip on the last lap but was able to reclaim the place from Alpine's Pierre Gasly at the end of the long straight.

And there was more drama at Ferrari as Charles Leclerc earned a 10-second penalty for tipping Lewis Hamilton into a spin.

Earlier, Hamilton had been given a 10-second penalty of his own for passing Norris off the track in a fight for position that also involved Leclerc.

It was a grand prix more reminiscent of American oval racing than Formula 1, and it depended on unique circumstances revolving around the Las Vegas circuit and energy-starved hybrid engines this year.

But there was no questioning the showbiz value in the city that prides itself as the entertainment capital of the world.

The key stories of an engrossing race were:

Verstappen's remarkable intelligence and control in the lead in the most demanding of circumstances

Another dip in a dreadful season for Russell

More controversy at Ferrari, as both drivers earned 10-second penalties for driving infringements in battles involving the other

Hamilton-Leclerc collision 'completely unacceptable'

"How many overtakes did I do?" Verstappen asked his engineer on the slowing down lap, as he reflected on a race the like of which F1 has not seen since the famous Monza slipstreaming battles of the 1960s and early 1970s.

"Yeah, and not many of them on the straight," his new engineer Tom Hart said, summing up how Verstappen had secured the win against the Mercedes challenge.

Lap after lap after lap, Verstappen, who started from pole, would lose the lead to Russell on the Strip only to reclaim it at the last corner, usually going around the outside.

If that did not work, and Russell passed later in the lap, or led across the line, Verstappen developed a trademark move around the outside of Turn Three to get back in front.

The race went on and on like that, punctuated by a mid-grand prix safety car, but through it all Verstappen always seemed in control.

As the race wore on, Antonelli came into the picture after starting sixth, and passed Russell with 12 laps to go to become Verstappen's main challenger.

Now it was the Italian's turn to swap places with Verstappen, but again the Dutchman had the measure of Mercedes.

At one point, Verstappen asked his team to come up with a better deployment strategy for the final lap because he thought Mercedes had "figured it out".

They came back to him to say that he had already come up with the best approach.

In the end, though, he need not have worried, as his rivals behind him gave him enough of a gap at the start of the final lap to not have to worry too much about defending his lead.

That critical final phase started with Russell deciding to make a move to become Verstappen's challenger again.

Russell went for a move into Turn Five with two laps to go but he locked up his brakes over the bumps heading into the corner - bumps that had earlier taken Red Bull's Isack Hadjar out of the lead battle when his front wing broke over them - and went straight on into the barrier.

Russell managed to reverse out of the barrier, but a ninth-place finish was not what he was expecting.

The incident was also unfortunate for him in the context of his calling out Verstappen's driving after qualifying, when he said "somebody has got to stand up to that guy".

Verstappen had the last word, both on track and literally. After seeing Russell's embarrassing mistake, Verstappen came on the radio to say: "Hah, hah. Well done. My God."

Now Antonelli looked to be the man who would challenge Verstappen for the win.

But that was counting without the McLarens. Piastri had already driven an outstanding race to recover from starting 17th because of an engine penalty and Norris had at one point dropped out of the top 10 in the chaotic lead battle in the first part of the grand prix.

But they were third and fourth around the penultimate lap and in what looked like a co-ordinated attack but certainly wasn't, both swept around Antonelli around the outside of the fast final corner heading into the last lap.

That gave Verstappen breathing space, and Antonelli was delayed sufficiently that he could not recover to challenge them.

Second-placed Norris summed it up, saying: "I think that must have been the most chaotic race ever in the history of Formula 1. I didn't know what was happening half the time."

A hectic end to the season means Formula 1 moves from Las Vegas to the Middle East next weekend, for the Qatar Grand Prix at the Lusail International Circuit from 27-29 November.

items.title: Verstappen's superb racecraft & Russell's costly mistake - driver ratings
items.content: <article>BBC Radio 5 Live F1 commentator Harry Benjamin rates how the drivers performed during the Las Vegas Grand Prix weekend.</article>
items.lbText:
Max Verstappen sealed his fourth win of the season with a stunning victory at a chaotic Las Vegas Grand Prix.

The Red Bull driver fought off his rivals for the lead throughout the race and crossed the line ahead of the two McLarens of Lando Norris and Oscar Piastri.

George Russell, who started second, locked up late on attempting a move on Mercedes team-mate Kimi Antonelli and finished ninth, while Charles Leclerc was given a 10-second time penalty for making contact with Ferrari team-mate Lewis Hamilton.

Here are my ratings for how the drivers performed across the whole weekend in Vegas.

A superb display of racecraft. Inherited pole after Kimi Antonelli's grid penalty and spent virtually the entire race being attacked, passed and then finding a way back through, while also working out the optimum energy deployment from inside his Red Bull. One of his finest victories.

A remarkable recovery after dropping as low as 11th in the madness of the opening part of the race. Had genuine pace throughout and fought all the way back to second, finishing less than a second behind Verstappen.

One of the drives of the race. Qualified seventh but started 17th because of his engine penalty and charged all the way through to the podium, gaining 14 places and joining McLaren team-mate Norris in passing Antonelli right at the end.

Fastest of everyone in qualifying and a genuine contender for victory despite starting sixth because of his engine penalty. Battled Verstappen superbly before his Mercedes' energy deployment problem on the final lap cost him two places, although he still recovered fourth from Pierre Gasly before the flag.

An excellent weekend and comfortably Alpine's best result of the season. Reached Q3, stayed with the leading group throughout and was less than three seconds away from victory at the finish.

Another huge result for Alpine. Qualified inside the top 10, stayed out of trouble while plenty around him didn't and converted ninth on the grid into sixth place.

A messy weekend but there was still plenty of fight in the race. Missing Q3 was disappointing and the 10-second time penalty for passing Norris off the circuit was harsh, although being spun by Ferrari team-mate Charles Leclerc later on was not his fault and he recovered to finish seventh.

A superb recovery from 20th on the grid after his power-unit penalty. Kept himself in contention throughout, made up 12 places and even pinched eighth from Russell at the line to secure Williams' joint-best result of the season.

For 48 laps this was heading towards a very high score. Fastest in both second and final practice, qualified third and spent most of the race going toe-to-toe with Verstappen for the lead. But locking up and putting it into the barrier with two laps remaining was an enormous and costly mistake.

A frustrating weekend from start to finish. Ferrari's qualifying struggles left him 11th and although he recovered well enough to finish sixth on the road, spinning his team-mate Hamilton earned a 10-second time penalty and dropped him to 10th.

Verstappen wins extraordinary race as Ferraris collide

Verstappen a constant amid chaos as he says Russell is 'so far below my level'

Hamilton-Leclerc collision 'completely unacceptable'

A solid weekend without quite finding the points. Led Audi in qualifying and again in the race, eventually finishing 11th after spending much of the evening embroiled in the midfield fight.

Similar story to team-mate Hulkenberg but just a little further back. Started 13th, finished 12th and narrowly held off Haas' Oliver Bearman at the flag.

A very good recovery after starting last because of power-unit penalties. Climbed nine positions, raced aggressively with both Audis and finished only two-tenths behind Bortoleto.

Qualified eighth and had looked set for another strong result before a fuel leak forced him to start from the pit lane. Recovering to 15th after effectively beginning the race out of contention was a decent salvage job.

The final position tells almost none of the story. Qualified fifth, started fourth and was part of the lead fight until his Red Bull front wing failed over the bumps after the safety-car restart. The pace was there for a huge result. He lost a position after the race because of a 10-second penalty for driving slowly and holding up Russell before they pitted under the safety car.

Another respectable showing in only his second grand prix for Haas. Narrowly missed Q2 and was running steadily before being spun in the Sergio Perez collision, then recovered from the back after the safety car to finish 16th.

Another difficult weekend for Aston Martin. Qualified 20th before his engine penalty pushed him further back and there was little progress to be made during the race.

Qualified at the back and Cadillac again lacked the pace to threaten the midfield. At least he stayed in the fight with the Aston Martins and made it to the finish after several recent retirements.

Aston Martin simply never looked competitive. Qualified 19th, spent the race towards the back and retired late on.

A real missed opportunity for the Briton and his Racing Bulls team. Sixth in qualifying and fifth on the grid was superb, and he was still right in the leading train when the safety car came out. Spinning while trying to warm the tyres behind it and eventually retiring was a costly unforced error.

Qualified only 18th but appeared to have better race pace and was making progress before the collision with Camara ended his afternoon.

A weekend that ended before the race even started. Qualified 16th and was due to start 14th, but overheating rear brakes on the laps to the grid caused enough damage to prevent Williams from racing the car.

items.title: Hamilton-Leclerc collision completely unacceptable, says Ferrari boss
items.content: <article>Ferrari drivers Lewis Hamilton and Charles Leclerc face yet another tense discussion over their ability to race together cleanly on track after colliding in Las Vegas.</article>
items.lbText:
Ferrari drivers Lewis Hamilton and Charles Leclerc face yet another tense discussion over their ability to race together cleanly on track after colliding in the Las Vegas Grand Prix.

Leclerc tipped Hamilton into a spin with 22 laps to go, costing both points in a race where at one stage they were racing with the McLarens, which finished on the podium.

Leclerc was given a 10-second penalty for the incident, which meant he finished 10th, three places behind Hamilton, in a race won by Red Bull's Max Verstappen.

It was the second race-compromising incident within grands prix, and it came after the drivers had been brought together to clear the air at the last race in Brazil after their first-lap fighting in Mexico cost them a win.

Hamilton said such an incident "should never happen" but added that: "The question should be for Ferrari now."

Leclerc said: "We just need to fix whatever is not working."

Team principal Frederic Vasseur described the situation as "completely unacceptable".

Verstappen wins extraordinary race as Ferraris collide

The Frenchman said: "It's a lack of respect for the team, for the sponsor, the same speech as after Mexico.

"We passed the message to Charles to not overtake because in this kind of race you have to overtake the cars in front of you or you're passed by others. It means you have to do your race and Charles clearly made a mistake.

"It's penalising the team a lot and it's completely unacceptable. Honestly we are more than upset because that message was clear after Mexico, we had a chat together in Brazil, today we passed the message to think about the team when racing together and the outcome is this one."

The battle between the two drivers has been tense all season, and in the second part of the year there have been a series of flashpoints, whether it be on-track racing, disputes about how best to work through strategy, and Hamilton ignoring two separate calls to pit in different races, both of which compromised his result, because he was looking at beating Leclerc.

Hamilton said: "It's not something I want to really get into."

The seven-time champion, who struggled against Leclerc last year but who has been revived in 2026, deflected questions about whether he should be given number-one status.

"I've never asked to be number one," he said. "I genuinely haven't ever asked.

"There was a point in the season where I was 40-odd points ahead, and at that point, the fight was with me and Kimi (Antonelli).

"I was the closest one to him. I was second for a long time in the year.

"At that point, we needed backing to make sure we beat Kimi. There were a few instances in the season where, with the support, I think we could have beaten Kimi.

"But no, that's not what I've asked for. We shouldn't have gotten together. That should just never happen. But I've said everything I can on it, and the question should be for Ferrari now."

Before the incident, the drivers expressed their differing views on team radio, Leclerc expressing his concern for the way Hamilton was defending, Hamilton saying they should be focused on catching the cars in front.

Leclerc said: "He needs to be careful with this squeezing because it's not going to end well."

Hamilton swore as he asked the team to tell Leclerc to "back off", adding: "I'm trying to catch these guys ahead."

This was similar to their different stances in Mexico, when Leclerc was attacking Hamilton on the first lap while the Briton felt they should be working together to defend their one-two positions.

Vasseur said he would talk to the drivers the day after the race, once the immediate heat of the situation had dissipated.

"You can't imagine the frustration for me, but more important for the guys at home," Vasseur said.

"I want to have a discussion tomorrow. Also, Charles to digest the situation. It's not the right place to discuss with them two minutes after the race."

Leclerc said: "I don't think it's going to be intense. None of our discussions were intense, but surely it cannot continue like that.

"I've taken a penalty, so I guess the blame is on me from the stewards and I guess from the majority, so as a result I guess it was deserved."

items.title: 'Somebody has to stand up to that guy' - Verstappen-Russell rivalry blows up again
items.content: <article>The George Russell-Max Verstappen feud surfaced again in Las Vegas, adding spice to a race where they will start on the front row.</article>
items.lbText:
The Las Vegas Grand Prix will start with two drivers on the front row who dislike each other - and after qualifying one said of the other that "somebody has got to stand up to that guy".

"That guy" is Max Verstappen, who starts his Red Bull from pole position. The driver criticising him is Mercedes' George Russell, who lines up second.

Both were promoted after the fastest qualifier, new world champion Kimi Antonelli, was demoted by a five-place grid penalty for exceeding his engine allocation for the season.

Russell's beef stemmed from an incident in final practice, in which Verstappen overtook the Mercedes on the Las Vegas Strip, then veered in front of him into Turn 14.

Russell, unhappy with the Dutchman's behaviour, dived down the Red Bull's inside on braking for the corner, got alongside, and then made his displeasure known by pushing Verstappen wide, the two cars making light contact.

They were called to the stewards to discuss the incident. Verstappen was given a warning having been found to have made an "unpredictable change of direction under braking".

After qualifying, Russell told Sky Italia: "I think the warning was fine. There's nothing in the rules to say that you cannot overtake someone who is starting their lap but when you do this, you are screwing this person over.

"He does this week in, week out, with many drivers. Everybody accepts it and I am not just going to accept somebody to screw me over like this and walk around like they are bigger and better than everyone else. Somebody has got to stand up to that guy."

Russell's comments were not put to Verstappen as he had finished his media commitments by the time they emerged into wider knowledge in Las Vegas.

Asked about the incident in the official news conference, Verstappen said: "Nothing happened."

When Verstappen spoke to the Dutch media, he was again reluctant to be drawn on it.

But asked whether it gave him extra motivation to beat Russell in the race, he said: "I don't need any extra motivation."

These two have history. This incident is almost exactly two years since they fell out in public following a row at the Qatar Grand Prix where Verstappen felt Russell had stepped over the line to get him a penalty that demoted him from pole position.

They exchanged insults. Russell, in remarks that echo those from Las Vegas, said: "People have been bullied by Max for years now."

Verstappen called Russell a "backstabber" and a "loser".

That was just the latest in a series of incidents - after a clash in Azerbaijan in 2022, Verstappen called Russell "Princess George" in a spat the Briton called "a little bit pathetic".

And then there was the 2025 Spanish Grand Prix. Late in the race, with Verstappen struggling with his tyres, they banged wheels as Russell attempted an overtake.

Verstappen retained the position after going off track and after being told by his team to hand the position to Russell, he moved over for the Mercedes and then appeared back on its inside and made contact with it.

He was penalised 10 seconds for that, and the following day issued a public apology for his behaviour.

All this certainly adds a hefty dose of extra spice to a race which, frankly, needs it.

This is the first of three 'dead rubbers' to close the season now both championships have been settled. There is little to fight for, and very little enthusiasm in the paddock for the final two races in the war-torn Middle East.

Despite widespread disquiet about going to Qatar and Abu Dhabi, everyone has been towing the party line on that one recently in public, that they trust governing body the FIA and Formula 1 to have made the right decision.

After qualifying, though, Verstappen came close to becoming the first to break the omerta, when he told the Dutch media "of course I would rather be at home", before repeating that he trusted the sport's bosses on the matter.

BBC Sport has been told of at least one other major driver who would rather not be going to the Middle East specifically because of concerns about safety.

As for the racing here in Sin City, it is set up beautifully.

The two drivers on the front row, as well as not troubling to hide their distaste for each other, are also the only two to have won here.

Verstappen has won two of the three events on the Strip circuit, sandwiching Russell's victory in 2024.

In theory, that could give an opportunity to McLaren's Lando Norris, who qualified fourth, and starts third as a result of Antonelli's penalty.

But the 2025 world champion was concerned about the McLaren's lack of straight-line speed.

"The pace in the car is not bad," he said. "The car is performing well, but our straight-line speed is so far off that we are not going to be able to overtake someone, so I think it's going to be a tough day."

Antonelli fastest but penalty leaves Verstappen on pole

Drivers limited to 27 laps for tyres in Qatar

His team principal Andrea Stella was more optimistic.

McLaren's battle with Red Bull for third in the constructors' championship - the two are separated by just 17 points - is one of the few major issues still to be settled this year.

Stella saw the fact that Norris had missed out on beating Russell by just 0.02secs, despite having a plastic bag caught in his floor that he said had cost 0.1secs, as reason for optimism.

As were the lessons of the Italian Grand Prix - held on a track with similarly long straights and big braking zones.

"We saw that because of this towing effect you actually can stay tangled, linked to the other cars," Stella said. "So we are definitely looking forward to tomorrow and encouraged by the fact that qualifying has been competitive.

"Because the tow effect is so big and because it's bigger than Monza, racing will be difficult to predict.

"So we need to make sure that from a driver's team point of view, we are ready for all the situations.…

items.title: Antonelli fastest but penalty leaves Verstappen on pole
items.content: <article>Mercedes' Kimi Antonelli is fastest in qualifying for the Las Vegas Grand Prix but a grid penalty hands pole position to Red Bull's Max Verstappen.</article>
items.lbText:
Mercedes' Kimi Antonelli was fastest in qualifying for the Las Vegas Grand Prix but a grid penalty will hand pole position to Red Bull's Max Verstappen.

Antonelli, running at the back of the pack of cars in qualifying and maximising his tow, beat Verstappen by 0.258 seconds.

But the new world champion has a five-place grid penalty for using more than permitted number of engine components and will start sixth.

The Italian's team-mate George Russell was just 0.073secs behind Verstappen and will start alongside the Dutchman on the front row.

McLaren's Lando Norris qualified fourth, and will start third, ahead of Red Bull's Isack Hadjar.

Both Ferraris were eliminated in the second session and qualified 11th and 12th with Charles Leclerc ahead of Lewis Hamilton.

Each will be promoted a place by a 10-place penalty for McLaren's Oscar Piastri, who qualified seventh.

Racing Bulls' rookie Arvid Lindblad, sixth fastest, is the last driver to be promoted as a result of Antonelli's penalty.

Racing Bulls' Liam Lawson will start seventh with Alpine's Pierre Gasly eighth and Franco Colapinto ninth.

Drivers limited to 27 laps for tyres in Qatar

Antonelli's final run did not start auspiciously as he and Russell became tangled up with the Alpines and Racing Bulls as they sought the best track position to optimise the slipstream effect.

Antonelli ended up the last driver to run and made it to the line with only one second to spare before the chequered flag, one second behind Lindblad.

Normally, being so close to the car in front would be a compromise but in Las Vegas it magnified the tow effect and Antonelli leapt to the front. "That was all the tow," he said over the radio after being told he was on pole.

"Starting the lap, I was only one second behind the car in front and I thought I was screwed," he said. "But the tow is so powerful here."

Verstappen, who has won two of the three Las Vegas Grands Prix, said: "I have been struggling with some weird issues that were also in the car in Brazil and just trying to get my head around how to deal with that.

"In qualifying we managed to make it work. Had a solid qualifying. My first lap in qualifying was pretty much as good as it could be with the tow, so to be on the front row is good for us.

"It was solid in the corners, and you have a bit of dirty air, but it is insane how much you gain on the straights."

Russell had looked in the running for the pole, but was happy with his session despite missing out.

"Overall it's been a very solid session and a solid day," he said.

"I wanted to be on pole but I am probably more pleased with the performance than in Mexico when I was on the front row.

"Kimi did a great job and he probably thought it wasn't going to work out so well being so close but with the tow it worked out."

Leclerc and Hamilton were separated by 0.056 seconds and both had tales of woe that explained their early exit - but very different ones.

Leclerc said: "Just a very poor qualifying. We are losing one second in the straights which makes it difficult enough already, and then I did a mistake when I had to put the lap in in Q2, following multiple mistakes we have done as a team and this we need to look at because it builds a lot of frustration that doesn't help.

"But in the end the mistake is on me and I will look at that."

Hamilton added: "It was a nightmare. Just low grip, felt like the tyres weren't working, had some damage on the floor that appeared out of nowhere and was losing 0.3-0.4secs and then had a deployment issue that lost us 0.6secs and with that we were nowhere, and I had no-one ahead of me. That wasn't great. So everything wasn't great.

"We knew we would struggle a bit here but maybe more than we anticipated."

items.title: Drivers limited to 27 laps for tyres in Qatar
items.content: <article>Formula 1 drivers will be limited to a maximum of 27 laps on a set of tyres at next weekend's Qatar Grand Prix.</article>
items.lbText:
Formula 1 drivers will be limited to a maximum of 27 laps on a set of tyres at next weekend's Qatar Grand Prix.

The decision is caused by concern over the integrity of the Pirelli tyres on the high-speed Lusail track, which has a series of demanding, long-duration corners.

It means teams will have to make at least two pit stops during the 57-lap grand prix, as was the case last year.

The limit applies on a single set of tyres whenever it is used across sessions.

So mileage done in practice or qualifying, for example, would limit the number of laps that could be done on a set of tyres in the race.

Pirelli said the limit was longer then last year's 25 laps because of the reduced downforce levels of the 2026 cars compared with 2025.

"The increase has been made possible by the lower load levels recorded so far on the current generation of cars and by a further reinforcement of the tyre construction," a statement said.

Last year, the limit led to a major strategic error by McLaren, who lost a win because they failed to pit under a safety car period when everyone else did.

It is the third time in four years Pirelli has imposed a tyre-duration limit at Qatar, where running wide over flat kerbs in addition to the high-speed nature of the track is especially demanding for the tyres.

Pirelli described the decision as a "precautionary measure" that was "linked to the unique characteristics of the Lusail circuit, which is particularly demanding in terms of energy loads, thermal stress and tread wear".

In terms of the way the limit will be imposed, the statement said: "Laps will be counted cumulatively across all track sessions, including any laps completed under the safety car or virtual safety car.

"As far as the grand prix is concerned, all laps completed from the start signal to the chequered flag will count towards the total.

"Reconnaissance laps, formation laps and any laps completed after the end of the race will not be included.

"In all other track sessions, any lap that has been started but not completed will nevertheless be counted as a full lap.

"Should a team assemble a tyre set using tyres that have covered different mileages, the tyre with the highest lap count will determine the mileage attributed to that set."

items.title: F1 bosses agree V8 engines deal from 2030
items.content: <article>Formula 1 bosses reach a deal that means V8 turbo hybrid engines will replace the current controversial units in 2030.</article>
items.lbText:
Formula 1 bosses are close to a deal that will see V8 turbo hybrid engines replace the current controversial engines in 2030.

McLaren chief executive officer Zak Brown said an "agreement in principle" had been reached by engine manufacturers and F1 bosses on the new rules.

These will be for a 2.1-litre V8 turbo engine with a smaller electrical element than this year, as first revealed by BBC Sport last month.

Some details remain to be resolved but the main core of the rules has been agreed.

The electrical element will be for a maximum power output of 200kW - compared with 350kW this year.

But only half of that will be available at all times, with the remaining half used only for an overtake mode.

A key element of the rules will be to remove the issue of energy starvation that has been criticised by the drivers this year for taking away "pure" racing.

But the overall power output of the engines will be similar to now.

The combustion engine will have about 780bhp, while 200kW is 270bhp.

That means a total power output of 1,050bhp in overtake mode or just over 900bhp in standard running.

Brown said: "Everyone is very, very excited. Now it's about kind of dotting the i's and crossing the t's.

"I'm excited for the new engines, I think everyone will be, the power units. But there's a lot more also going on to continue to evolve the sport. So, between the FIA and Formula 1, they're doing a great job."

Russell fastest in Las Vegas practice after rain

How to follow Las Vegas Grand Prix on the BBC

Alpine executive director Flavio Briatore said: "We have the agreement, basically. It's not signed, but it looks like everybody's agreed to 2030 V8s, and I'm very happy.

"It's the right way to go. We need an engine with a lot of noise, and a simple engine, and we need to be racing with that."

The ruleset amounts to a compromise reached by manufacturers after FIA president Mohammed Ben Sulayem initially pushed for a naturally aspirated engine without turbo or electrical components.

But these were required to reduce overall fuel consumption, and therefore weight at the start of races.

That means Ben Sulayem's desire for a return to the loud volumes of the previous V8 era from 2006 to 2013 will not be achieved. The engines are expected to sound similar to now.

This was important because a significant increase in engine noise would have put at threat some races in city centres that are commercially important to F1, such as Miami and Las Vegas.

The 2.1-litre capacity has been arrived at because it amounts to adding to two cylinders to the current 1.6-litre V6 blocks, with the aim of reducing development costs.

Cars are expected to start races with about 110-120kg of fuel, up from about 100kg now. A total weight limit of 150kg for the power-units will be imposed, down by about 30kg from the current engines.

There will be a fuel energy flow limit to keep the power of the combustion engine under control, and a budget cap figure for engines set at $190m (£145m) per year.

As part of negotiations, General Motors, backers of the Cadillac team, will delay the production of its new engine until 2030. It had been scheduled for 2029.

In return, GM will lose its voting rights on current engine rules and be classified as a new manufacturer from 2030.

The team will continue to use Ferrari customer engines through 2029.

Cadillac F1 chief executive officer Dan Towriss said: "For a period of time, we were working on both. So, they've already got a V6 base to build off of, and working towards the V8.

"There are a number of designs that are in motion now, and so there's a lot of good foundation for what we're trying to build and the direction we're headed in."

items.title: The art of protection - inside an F1 helmet factory
items.content: <article>Inside the extraordinary world of Formula 1 helmets, where precision engineering, personal expression and life-saving technology join forces.</article>
items.lbText:
As soft, instrumental opera music plays in the background of a precise temperature-controlled room in northern Italy, Thomaso is using a children's toy ball and hairdryer to perform his meticulous work.

Hugely focused, in a crisp white coat, he moulds a precious sticky black material over and over again for up to six hours.

One day, his fastidiousness may save the life of one of the best athletes in the world.

The room Thomaso works in is called "the magic shop". Its motto? 'One man, one shell.'

Much of what happens inside is top secret. What we can say is the black material Thomaso is working with is a blend of carbon fibre that has to be stored at exactly -16°C. He moulds it into a secret form, layer by layer, after which the entire unit is baked in a vacuum bag at a set pressure at 120C for three-and-a-half hours.

The handmade products he is working on are personally chosen by their clients - for their safety features, as well as comfort, practicality and look.

Thomaso's colleague Sven travels the world between February and December to keep those clients happy. A different country almost every week, with a reliable weather forecast almost as important as a large allowance of hand luggage.

Together with 32 colleagues, Thomaso and Sven work for one of the four leading manufacturers of F1 helmets.

They produce sophisticated engineering masterpieces, and works of art.

"Our philosophy is to make the best product for the best drivers," says chief executive Alberto Dall'Oglio.

In the early days of grand prix racing, protection was rudimentary. Drivers often wore little more than leather flying caps, goggles and - eventually - relatively basic open-face helmets.

Safety standards were inconsistent, materials primitive and the consequences of an accident frequently devastating.

According to the official F1 website, Giuseppe Farina - the first winner of an F1 race and first world champion - competed wearing nothing more than "his trusty cloth cap, two pairs of goggles (he wore the spare pair round his neck), cotton dungarees, leather boots and leather gloves".

The arrival of the full-face helmet in the late 1960s marked a defining moment. Bell introduced its pioneering Star model in 1966, and Dan Gurney became the first driver to race in a full-face helmet in 1968. The face - previously exposed to flying debris, fire and impact - finally had meaningful protection.

Progress was painfully slow, and motorsport's darkest moments repeatedly exposed the limitations of the technology.

In 1976, Niki Lauda 's Ferrari erupted into flames at the Nurburgring. His helmet came loose, leaving his head exposed to the fire. He survived, but suffered severe burns and lifelong injuries. The accident became a defining lesson in the importance of helmet retention, fire resistance and the protection of the driver's entire head.

The tragic deaths of Roland Ratzenberger and Ayrton Senna at Imola in 1994, followed by Jules Bianchi's fatal accident at Suzuka in 2014, demonstrated even increasingly sophisticated helmets could not eliminate every danger.

Ratzenberger suffered a fatal basilar skull fracture; Senna succumbed to multiple fractures of the skull base, after a strut from the suspension pierced his helmet.

Bianchi's accident exposed the vulnerability of drivers' heads to heavy external impacts. Helmets are only one part of a much wider safety system, which now includes stronger survival cells, the Hans device and the halo.

In 2004, the FIA introduced its new helmet safety standard, requiring advanced carbon-fibre construction to deliver greater strength, improved impact protection and reduced weight for F1 drivers.

At Bahrain's Sakhir circuit in 2020, Romain Grosjean's Haas split apart against the barriers and burst into flames. After 28 seconds trapped in the wreckage, he emerged with burns to his hands and ankles. His Bell helmet, fire-resistant equipment and the halo were instrumental in saving his life - a powerful testament to decades of safety innovation and engineering.

"Today's helmets are withstanding up to 30 seconds at 700, even 800, degrees," says Dall'Oglio. "Then they have to self-extinguish within 15 seconds."

Dall'Oglio is the CEO of Schuberth Performance, Thomaso an engineer and Sven a racing service technician, working trackside at more than 400 grands prix, preparing helmets and visors for rain, sun or floodlights.

Needing to avoid any impact on the helmets, he must carry them - sometimes five or six at a time - to races.

Schuberth, a German firm, has a long history in head protection. Founded in 1922, the company began making industrial products before moving into helmet linings in the late 1920s, then mining and motorcycle helmets in the 1950s.

With its HQ in Magdeburg and F1 helmet production in Schio, northern Italy, it produces special helmets for military forces - made of Kevlar, and some of a similar carbon - in the same factory as the F1 helmets.

Its motorsport credentials grew considerably around the turn of the millennium.

Following Michael Schumacher's British Grand Prix accident in 1999, Schuberth developed a new generation of racing helmets, subsequently worn by Schumacher and other leading drivers.

Of the current drivers, four-time world champion Max Verstappen is the most prominent to wear a Schuberth helmet. He is joined by Red Bull team-mate Isack Hadjar, Cadillac's Sergio Perez, Audi's Nico Hulkenberg and Arvid Lindblad at Racing Bulls.

Dall'Oglio's team hand-makes about 250 helmets a year.

An F1 helmet is a remarkable marriage of science and aesthetics.

Constructed using advanced composite materials, including carbon fibre, it must be exceptionally strong while remaining light enough to minimise strain on a driver's neck.

Visors, ventilation systems, fire-resistant linings, communication equipment, a straw-like drinks system and carefully designed retention mechanisms all contribute to its performance.…

items.title: F1 to introduce full-time race stewards from 2027
items.content: <article>Formula 1's governing body the FIA is to introduce permanent race stewards from the 2027 season.</article>
items.lbText:
Formula 1's governing body the FIA is to introduce permanent race stewards from the 2027 season.

The move follows consistent calls from grand prix drivers for the change because of criticisms of inconsistency of decisions regarding penalties for on-track incidents.

The FIA said in a statement that it would begin recruiting permanent stewards, and was planning a "phased introduction" during the 2027 season.

The FIA statement added: "The introduction of dedicated full-time stewards to the FIA's flagship championship will provide continuity and expertise within the stewarding structure, further advancing the FIA's commitment to fairness through the ongoing review and continuous improvement of sporting regulations and stewarding guidelines.

"It will also allow for deeper implementation of best practice and greater consistency in decision-making."

It said that the use of driver stewards, usually an ex-F1 driver, would continue, "recognising the invaluable expertise they bring".

The plan is for "a small number" of full-time stewards to be recruited during 2027 and the group to be expanded from 2028.

"Existing FIA stewards will continue to play a vital role, contributing their experience within a mixed roster of full-time and part-time stewards for the foreseeable future," the statement said.

In reality, the move is not a major step on from the current situation, where a small number of stewards are rotated around races.

Each grand prix has a group of four stewards, one of which is an ex-driver.

Current drivers have often referenced the fact that they had repeatedly complained during briefings with FIA officials that rulings on driver standards and racing errors were not applied on a consistent basis.

Last year, Williams driver Carlos Sainz, a director of drivers' body the Grand Prix Drivers' Association, said: "F1 and the FIA all agree that [permanent stewards] should be the way forward, where at least two of the three stewards are permanent and we have one rotational for teaching purposes."

The decision follows the opening of an FIA race operations centre at F1's Biggin Hill headquarters in south London.

The FIA has in recent years received increased income from F1 - which provides the majority of its funding - on the basis that this would be applied to improving officialdom and rule-making.

FIA president Mohammed Ben Sulayem said: "This latest major investment in FIA officiating reflects our dedication to delivering the highest standards of decision-making, fairness and integrity in motorsport.

"The recruitment of full-time stewards is a significant step in our longstanding mission of building a dedicated officiating ecosystem in the FIA Formula 1 World Championship, it is also an investment in the future of our sport."

items.title: Verstappen 'trusts' F1 over Middle East decision
items.content: <article>Max Verstappen says he trusts in Formula 1 after their decision to end the season in the Middle East, despite the ongoing conflicts in the area. </article>
items.lbText:
Max Verstappen says he "trusts" Formula 1 has made the right decision in pressing ahead with the final two races of the season in the Middle East.

Last week, F1 stood down preparations for a substitute race at Imola in Italy if the events in Qatar and Abu Dhabi could not be held because of ongoing conflicts in the area.

The sport will now conclude the season in the Middle East, unless the situation deteriorates before the Qatar event on 27-29 November and Abu Dhabi on 4-6 December.

Verstappen said: "I trust F1 and FIA to make the right call on that, right?

"I don't have all the intel. I'm not an officer. I just hope that they make the right call on that. And that's all that you can rely on, really.

"They also send over their findings and understanding. So I trust them."

No trust problem with Ferrari team - Hamilton

How sporting events are being affected by Middle East conflict

Yamaha will not travel to Qatar for MotoGP race

Verstappen had previously voiced his opposition to ending the season in the Middle East.

"Normally I am happy to go to Qatar and Abu Dhabi, but you know, when there is a war nearby, and if some of the countries are in conflict with each other, then I think we shouldn't go," Verstappen said in September.

The Red Bull driver's fresh remarks reflect a uniform public stance in F1 on the situation, even though there are widespread misgivings among personnel about travelling to the Middle East in the context of the two conflicts in the area.

Last Sunday Iran targeted a US military base in Bahrain with a drone attack for the second time in three days, the latest salvo in the war launched against the country by the US and Israel in February.

And Houthi rebels in Yemen are advancing in their war against the Saudi-backed government of the country.

Missile attacks from the Houthis into Saudi Arabia are threatening that country's chances of hosting the second grand prix of next season, which is scheduled for 19-21 March.

McLaren's Lando Norris said that while he is "fine" with the decision to race, he is concerned about the "big team" behind him.

"I have my friend's wedding in Bahrain next week, so I was planning on going there and then going on to Qatar and then Abu Dhabi," he added.

"But it's not about me. It's a lot more people. It's the fans, it's the team personnel, so the question is for them, more than I would say it is for myself."

Mercedes driver George Russell said he has "no hesitation" in racing and that while he's "sure some people have their reservations" he doesn't "know of anyone who's concerned".

"I know people who live in the region and they said it quite bluntly, if they didn't feel comfortable they wouldn't be there with their families," he said.

"When you look around the world there are a lot of terrible things going on.

"You've just got to trust in the people. If they say it's safe, then you trust in them. F1 aren't stupid and I'm sure there's plans A, B, C, D, etc. So fingers crossed it'll all be fine."

MotoGP, which is owned by the same US group as F1, held a race in Qatar last weekend without problems.

F1, which has significant commercial links with the Middle East, has been closely monitoring the situation and has been advised by security officials and government figures in the Gulf and Europe that the races can go ahead, and there is no official advice against travelling to Qatar or Abu Dhabi.

F1 said in a statement last week that it was still prepared to cancel the two races in Qatar and Abu Dhabi if the situation deteriorated.

"If the situation develops negatively in the coming weeks before the events in the Middle East, we will not hesitate to do the right thing and the safety of everyone will always be the priority," an F1 spokesperson said on Tuesday.
